claim: The first cases of Zika virus (ZIKV) in Brazil were concurrently reported in March 2015 in Camaçari city in the state of Bahia and in Natal, the state capital city of Rio Grande do Norte.
source: The first cases of Zika virus (ZIKV) in Brazil were concurrently reported in March 2015 in Camaçari city in the state of Bahia (Campos et al., 2015) and in Natal, the state capital city of Rio Grande do Norte (Zanluca et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to two published studies (Campos et al., 2015 and Zanluca et al., 2015).

claim: During 2015, the epidemic in Camaçari quickly spread to other municipalities of the Bahia state, including the capital city of Salvador, which together accounted for over 90% of all notified Zika cases in Brazil in 2015.
source: During that year, the epidemic in Camaçari quickly spread to other municipalities of the Bahia state, including the capital city of Salvador, which together accounted for over 90% of all notified Zika cases in Brazil in 2015 (Faria et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2016a.

claim: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV, East Central South African genotype) was first introduced in 2014 in the city of Feira de Santana.
source: During this period, many local Bahia health services were overwhelmed by an ongoing Chikungunya virus (CHIKV, East Central South African genotype) epidemic, that was first introduced in 2014 in the city of Feira de Santana (FSA) (Nunes et al., 2015; Faria et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nunes et al., 2015 and Faria et al., 2016b.

claim: The rise in ZIKV incidence in FSA coincided temporally with an increase in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and microcephaly.
source: The rise in ZIKV incidence in FSA coincided temporally with an increase in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and microcephaly (Faria et al., 2016a), with an unprecedented total of 21 confirmed cases of microcephaly in FSA between January 2015 and May 2017.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2016a and data on confirmed microcephaly cases.

claim: There were 21 confirmed cases of microcephaly in FSA between January 2015 and May 2017.
source: The rise in ZIKV incidence in FSA coincided temporally with an increase in cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and microcephaly (Faria et al., 2016a), with an unprecedented total of 21 confirmed cases of microcephaly in FSA between January 2015 and May 2017.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: There is wide statistical support for a causal link between ZIKV and severe manifestations such as microcephaly.
source: There is wide statistical support for a causal link between ZIKV and severe manifestations such as microcephaly (Rubin et al., 2016; de Araújo et al., 2016; Soares de Araújo et al., 2016; Honein et al., 2017; Brasil et al., 2016; de Oliveira et al., 2017), and the proposed link in 2015 led to the declaration of the South American epidemic as an international public health emergency by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016; the response to which has been limited to vector control initiatives and advice to delay pregnancy in the affected countries (WHO, 2016b; WHO, 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The proposed link between ZIKV and microcephaly in 2015 led to the declaration of the South American epidemic as an international public health emergency by the WHO in 2016.
source: There is wide statistical support for a causal link between ZIKV and severe manifestations such as microcephaly (Rubin et al., 2016; de Araújo et al., 2016; Soares de Araújo et al., 2016; Honein et al., 2017; Brasil et al., 2016; de Oliveira et al., 2017), and the proposed link in 2015 led to the declaration of the South American epidemic as an international public health emergency by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016; the response to which has been limited to vector control initiatives and advice to delay pregnancy in the affected countries (WHO, 2016b; WHO, 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO documents.

claim: The WHO response to the ZIKV epidemic has been limited to vector control initiatives and advice to delay pregnancy in the affected countries.
source: There is wide statistical support for a causal link between ZIKV and severe manifestations such as microcephaly (Rubin et al., 2016; de Araújo et al., 2016; Soares de Araújo et al., 2016; Honein et al., 2017; Brasil et al., 2016; de Oliveira et al., 2017), and the proposed link in 2015 led to the declaration of the South American epidemic as an international public health emergency by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2016; the response to which has been limited to vector control initiatives and advice to delay pregnancy in the affected countries (WHO, 2016b; WHO, 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to WHO documents.

claim: Climate variables are critical for the epidemiological dynamics of Zika and other arboviral diseases, such as dengue and chikungunya.
source: Climate variables are critical for the epidemiological dynamics of Zika and other arboviral diseases, such as dengue (Lourenço and Recker, 2014; Feldstein et al., 2015; Kraemer et al., 2015; van Panhuis et al., 2015) and chikungunya (Poletti et al., 2011; Mourya et al., 2004; Salje et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: A low observation rate and high vectorial capacity translated into a significant attack rate during the 2015 outbreak in FSA.
source: Using a climate-driven transmission model and notified Zika case data, we show that a low observation rate and high vectorial capacity translated into a significant attack rate during the 2015 outbreak, with a subsequent decline in 2016 and fade-out in 2017 due to herd-immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the transmission model fitted to case data.

claim: There was a subsequent decline in ZIKV cases in 2016 and fade-out in 2017 due to herd-immunity in FSA.
source: Using a climate-driven transmission model and notified Zika case data, we show that a low observation rate and high vectorial capacity translated into a significant attack rate during the 2015 outbreak, with a subsequent decline in 2016 and fade-out in 2017 due to herd-immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the transmission model fitted to case data.

claim: There is a potential Zika-related, low risk for microcephaly per pregnancy, but with significant public health impact given high attack rates.
source: We find a potential Zika-related, low risk for microcephaly per pregnancy, but with significant public health impact given high attack rates.
evidence: The claim is based on the analysis of microcephaly cases and attack rates.

claim: The balance between the loss of herd-immunity and viral re-importation will dictate future transmission potential of Zika in FSA.
source: The balance between the loss of herd-immunity and viral re-importation will dictate future transmission potential of Zika in this urban setting.
evidence: The claim is based on projections from the transmission model.

claim: Weekly cases remained very low for the two months following the first notification, adding up to just 10 notified cases by the end of March 2015.
source: Weekly cases remained very low for the following two months, adding up to just 10 notified cases by the end of March that year (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing case data.

claim: A rapid increase in the number of ZIKV cases was observed in April 2015, coinciding with Micareta, a local carnival-like festival.
source: A rapid increase in the number of cases was observed in April, coinciding with Micareta, a local carnival-like festival that takes place across the urban centres of Bahia.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The ZIKV epidemic in FSA peaked in July 2015.
source: The epidemic peaked in July 2015, which was followed by a sharp decline in notified cases over the next 1–2 months.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The first epidemic wave in FSA was followed by a significantly smaller outbreak in 2016, peaking around March.
source: This first epidemic wave was followed by a significantly smaller outbreak in 2016, peaking around March, and an even smaller outbreak in 2017 with no discernable epidemic peak.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: There was an even smaller outbreak in 2017 with no discernable epidemic peak in FSA.
source: This first epidemic wave was followed by a significantly smaller outbreak in 2016, peaking around March, and an even smaller outbreak in 2017 with no discernable epidemic peak.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: Confirmed microcephaly cases were absent by November 2015, after which a small epidemic was observed with peak counts in January 2016.
source: Confirmed (and monthly aggregated) microcephaly (MC) cases were absent by November 2015, after which a small epidemic was observed with peak counts in January 2016.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: There was a time lag of 5–6 months (20–24 weeks) between the first reported Zika epidemic wave and the MC peak in case counts.
source: We found a time lag of 5–6 months (20–24 weeks) between the first reported Zika epidemic wave and the MC peak in case counts.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the temporal relationship between ZIKV and MC cases.

claim: The time lag between ZIKV infection and MC coincides with previous observations suggesting a link between the development of neurological complications in newborns and ZIKV infection during the second trimester.
source: This coincides with previous observations suggesting a link between the development of neurological complications in newborns and ZIKV infection during the second trimester (Faria et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2016a.

claim: The epidemic behaviour in FSA was in sharp contrast with trends observed in notified cases across Brazil as a whole, for which the second epidemic in 2016 was approximately 6 times larger than the one in 2015.
source: Overall, the epidemic behaviour in FSA was in sharp contrast with trends observed in notified cases across Brazil (BR) as a whole, for which the second epidemic in 2016 was approximately 6 times larger than the one in 2015 (Figure 1A), suggesting the Bahia state as a focus point in the emergence and initial spread of ZIKV in Brazil (Faria et al., 2016c; Faria et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing case data.

claim: The Bahia state was a focus point in the emergence and initial spread of ZIKV in Brazil.
source: Overall, the epidemic behaviour in FSA was in sharp contrast with trends observed in notified cases across Brazil (BR) as a whole, for which the second epidemic in 2016 was approximately 6 times larger than the one in 2015 (Figure 1A), suggesting the Bahia state as a focus point in the emergence and initial spread of ZIKV in Brazil (Faria et al., 2016c; Faria et al., 2016a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Faria et al., 2016c and Faria et al., 2016a.

claim: A clear temporal synchronization between country level and FSA case counts could be observed.
source: Nonetheless, a clear temporal synchronization between country level and FSA case counts could be observed.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: The age distribution of notified ZIKV cases in FSA suggested a higher proportion of cases between 20 and 50 years of age.
source: The age distribution of notified ZIKV cases in FSA suggested a higher proportion of cases between 20 and 50 years of age, but with no discernible differences between the two epidemics (Figure 1B, top panel).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing age distribution data.

claim: When corrected for the expected number of cases assuming an equal risk of infection per age class, the number of cases within the 20-50 age group was closer to most other groups (IRR close to 1).
source: However, when corrected for the expected number of cases assuming an equal risk of infection per age class, we found the number of cases within this age group to be closer to most other groups (incidence rate ratio, IRR, close to 1, Figure 1B, bottom panel).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing IRR data.

claim: The per capita case counts within the youngest age class (<1 years) appeared higher than expected, with an IRR significantly above 1.
source: The per capita case counts within the youngest age class (<1 years) appeared higher than expected, with an IRR significantly above 1 and also higher in 2016 (IRR = 4.4, 95% CI [2.8, 7.0]) than in 2015 (IRR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.5, 2.6]), possibly indicating biased reporting and/or health care seeking with increased awareness of the disease.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of age-stratified case data.

claim: The IRR in the youngest age class was higher in 2016 (IRR = 4.4, 95% CI [2.8, 7.0]) than in 2015 (IRR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.5, 2.6]).
source: The per capita case counts within the youngest age class (<1 years) appeared higher than expected, with an IRR significantly above 1 and also higher in 2016 (IRR = 4.4, 95% CI [2.8, 7.0]) than in 2015 (IRR = 1.95, 95% CI [1.5, 2.6]), possibly indicating biased reporting and/or health care seeking with increased awareness of the disease.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of age-stratified case data.

claim: There was a consistent trend towards reduced IRR in the elderly (>65 years), although with significant uncertainties.
source: There was also a consistent trend towards reduced IRR in the elderly (>65 years), although with significant uncertainties.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of age-stratified case data.

claim: A small increase in IRR could be detected in the 20–34 year olds, which could potentially be a signature of sexual transmission in this age group.
source: Finally, a small increase in IRR could be detected in the 20–34 year olds, which could potentially be a signature of sexual transmission in this age group (Gao et al., 2016; Carlson et al., 2016; Foy et al., 2011; Turmel et al., 2016; Yakob et al., 2016; Maxian et al., 2017; Moghadas et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of age-stratified case data and supported by citations to studies on sexual transmission.

claim: The spatial distribution of total notified cases for BR highlighted the expected clustering of ZIKV cases within the Bahia state by the end of 2015.
source: The spatial distribution of total notified cases for BR highlighted the expected clustering of ZIKV cases within the Bahia state by the end of 2015 as well as the wider geographical range by July 2016 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing spatial distribution data.

claim: The spatial distribution of total notified cases for BR showed a wider geographical range by July 2016.
source: The spatial distribution of total notified cases for BR highlighted the expected clustering of ZIKV cases within the Bahia state by the end of 2015 as well as the wider geographical range by July 2016 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing spatial distribution data.

claim: The difference in geographical range could explain the higher number of cases observed during the 2016 epidemic at the country level.
source: We speculate that the difference in geographical range could explain the higher number of cases observed during the 2016 epidemic at the country level.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Daily rainfall in FSA between 2013 and May 2017 showed erratic fluctuations with sporadic episodes of intense rain but without a clear seasonal trend.
source: The data showed erratic fluctuations in rainfall with sporadic episodes of intense rain but without a clear seasonal trend.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of climate data.

claim: Temperature in FSA presented a much clearer seasonal signature with fixed amplitudes between 22 and 27 degree Celsius, peaking between December and May.
source: Temperature, on the other hand, presented a much clearer seasonal signature with fixed amplitudes between 22 and 27 degree Celsius, peaking between December and May.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of climate data.

claim: Humidity showed an intermediate scenario and appeared correlated with periods of intense rainfall but negatively correlated with temperature.
source: Humidity showed an intermediate scenario and appeared correlated with periods of intense rainfall but negatively correlated with temperature.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of climate data.

claim: Mosquito lifespan and EIP showed seasonal oscillations with median values of around 9 and 5 days, respectively.
source: Mosquito lifespan and EIP are main drivers of vectorial capacity and both showed seasonal oscillations with median values of around 9 and 5 days, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), which are in line with ranges found in the literature (Trpis et al., 1995; Trpis and Hausermann, 1986; Andraud et al., 2012; Hugo et al., 2014 and Table 3).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and citations to literature.

claim: There was a strong negative temporal correlation between mosquito lifespan and EIP, with periods of longer EIP coinciding with shorter lifespans and vice-versa.
source: Importantly, there was a strong negative temporal correlation between these two variables, with periods of longer EIP coinciding with shorter lifespans and vice-versa.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of model estimates.

claim: The observation rate was very low with a median of just under 0.004 (median = 0.0039, 95% CI [0.0038–0.0041]).
source: Of particular interest here was the very low observation rate (Figure 3B), with a median of just under 0.004 (median = 0.0039, 95% CI [0.0038–0.0041]), which equates to less than 4 in 1000 infections having been notified during the epidemic in FSA.
evidence: The claim is based on MCMC parameter estimation and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: The observation rate equates to less than 4 in 1000 infections having been notified during the epidemic in FSA.
source: Of particular interest here was the very low observation rate (Figure 3B), with a median of just under 0.004 (median = 0.0039, 95% CI [0.0038–0.0041]), which equates to less than 4 in 1000 infections having been notified during the epidemic in FSA.
evidence: The claim is based on MCMC parameter estimation.

claim: Based on the estimated observation rate, there were around 2,700 Zika infections during the first 2 months, of which only 10 were notified.
source: That is, based on our estimates, there were around 2,700 Zika infections during the first 2 months, of which only 10 were notified.
evidence: The claim is based on applying the estimated observation rate to the notified case data.

claim: By the end of the first epidemic wave around 65% (95% CI [57.0–72.9]) of the population in FSA had been infected by the virus.
source: More importantly, when applying this rate to the total number of cases we found that by the end of the first epidemic wave around 65% (95% CI [57.0–72.9]) of the population in FSA had been infected by the virus.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates of attack rate.

claim: The high attack rate of around 65% is not unusual for Zika and is in general agreement with observations elsewhere.
source: This high attack rate is not unusual for Zika, however, and is in general agreement with observations elsewhere (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Table 3 which contains literature-based estimates.

claim: Nearly 65% of the population got infected by ZIKV by the end of 2015.
source: As illustrated by the cumulative attack rate in Figure 4A, and similar to estimates from other regions in the world (Table 3), nearly 65% of the population got infected by ZIKV by the end of 2015, which rose to over 75% (95% CI [76.9–84.3]) by the end of 2016.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: The attack rate rose to over 75% (95% CI [76.9–84.3]) by the end of 2016.
source: As illustrated by the cumulative attack rate in Figure 4A, and similar to estimates from other regions in the world (Table 3), nearly 65% of the population got infected by ZIKV by the end of 2015, which rose to over 75% (95% CI [76.9–84.3]) by the end of 2016.
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: This temporal phenomenon has also been observed for the chikungunya virus (CHKV) when it was first introduced into FSA in 2014.
source: Notably, this temporal phenomenon has also been observed for the chikungunya virus (CHKV) when it was first introduced into FSA in 2014 (Faria et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2016b.

claim: The difference between R0 and Re might explain the marked reduction in Zika cases in FSA in 2016, at a time when the virus was infecting large numbers of individuals elsewhere in the country.
source: This in turn might explain the marked reduction in Zika cases in FSA in 2016, at a time when the virus was infecting large numbers of individuals elsewhere in the country (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates and comparison with country-level data.

claim: Projecting into the future using average climate data showed that the mean effective reproductive number is expected to remain low and close to 1 for the next few years.
source: Projecting into the future using average climate data for this region showed that the mean effective reproductive number is expected to remain low and close to 1 for the next few years, suggesting a very weak potential for ZIKV endemicity in the near future.
evidence: The claim is based on model projections.

claim: The projections suggest a very weak potential for ZIKV endemicity in the near future.
source: Projecting into the future using average climate data for this region showed that the mean effective reproductive number is expected to remain low and close to 1 for the next few years, suggesting a very weak potential for ZIKV endemicity in the near future.
evidence: The claim is based on model projections.

claim: The sporadic nature of Zika cases in 2017 strongly suggest that herd immunity in this region is at a sufficiently high level to prevent sustained transmission.
source: In fact, the sporadic nature of Zika cases in 2017 strongly suggest that herd immunity in this region is at a sufficiently high level to prevent sustained transmission.
evidence: The claim is based on observed case data and model estimates of herd immunity.

claim: The ODE model matched both the dynamics and the sizes of the first two epidemic waves in FSA between 2015 and 2016 but failed to capture the small number of cases during 2017.
source: Crucially, this would also explain why our ODE model matched both the dynamics and the sizes of the first two epidemic waves in FSA between 2015 and 2016 but failed to capture the small number of cases during 2017 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model fit with observed data and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: Without external introductions of infectious individuals, the model predicted an epidemic fade-out by 2017, in accordance with the lack of notified cases after March 2017.
source: Without external introductions of infectious individuals (human or vector) our results predicted an epidemic fade-out by 2017, in accordance with the lack of notified cases after March 2017 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on model projections and observed case data, supported by Figure 4A.

claim: The potential for ZIKV to cause another outbreak or to establish itself endemically in FSA is strongly dependent on the frequency of re-introductions.
source: Our results showed that the potential for ZIKV to cause another outbreak or to establish itself endemically in FSA is strongly dependent on the frequency of re-introductions, whereby higher rates of external introductions might in fact help to sustain high levels of herd immunity, whereas infrequent introductions are more likely to result in notable outbreaks.
evidence: The claim is based on stochastic model projections.

claim: Higher rates of external introductions might help to sustain high levels of herd immunity, whereas infrequent introductions are more likely to result in notable outbreaks.
source: Our results showed that the potential for ZIKV to cause another outbreak or to establish itself endemically in FSA is strongly dependent on the frequency of re-introductions, whereby higher rates of external introductions might in fact help to sustain high levels of herd immunity, whereas infrequent introductions are more likely to result in notable outbreaks.
evidence: The claim is based on stochastic model projections.

claim: Semi-endemic behaviour was only observed in simulations with low introduction rates.
source: That is, semi-endemic behaviour was only observed in simulations with low introduction rates (Figure 4B–C), as these scenarios strike a fine balance between a low number of new cases affecting herd-immunity levels and population turnover.
evidence: The claim is based on stochastic model projections and supported by Figure 4B-C.

claim: High introduction rates quickly exhaust the remaining susceptible pool, resulting in very long periods without epidemic behaviours.
source: In contrast, high introduction rates quickly exhaust the remaining susceptible pool, resulting in very long periods without epidemic behaviours.
evidence: The claim is based on stochastic model projections.

claim: The percentage of symptomatic infections can be assumed to be close to 18% based on the Yap Island epidemic of 2007.
source: Based on the previously reported Yap Island epidemic of 2007 (Duffy et al., 2009), the percentage of symptomatic infections can be assumed to be close to 18%.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: If the proportion of infected symptomatic individuals seeking medical attention or the proportion being correctly diagnosed is less than 10%, or both between 15–20%, the observation rate of 3.9 per 1000 infections can easily be explained.
source: Figure 5A shows that if any of these proportions is less than 10%, or both between 15–20%, our observation rate of 3.9 per 1000 infections can easily be explained.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis and supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Using a conservative total of 21 confirmed MC cases in FSA, the estimated average risk is approximately 0.35% of pregnancies experiencing ZIKV infection.
source: In particular, using a conservative total of 21 confirmed MC cases in FSA, i.e. rejecting suspected or other complications, we estimate an average risk of approximately 0.35% of pregnancies experiencing ZIKV infection.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MC cases and estimated attack rate.

claim: Including the 3 foetal deaths where ZIKV infections were confirmed during pregnancy increases the risk to 0.39%.
source: Including the 3 foetal deaths where ZIKV infections were confirmed during pregnancy, i.e. using a total of 24 cases, only increased the risk to 0.39%.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MC cases and estimated attack rate.

claim: Based on the results from the fitting approach and using the average birth rates of FSA as guideline, on average 3–4 MC cases are expected per 100 k individuals at 65% exposure to the virus.
source: More generally, based on the results from our fitting approach and using the average birth rates of FSA as guideline, we estimate that on average 3–4 MC cases are expected per 100 k individuals at 65% exposure to the virus.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MC cases and estimated attack rate.

claim: Around 65% of the local population were predicted to have been infected by ZIKV during the first wave in 2015.
source: Based on this, around 65% of the local population were predicted to have been infected by ZIKV during the first wave in 2015, which is in the same range as the reported Zika outbreaks in French Polynesia (66%) (Cauchemez et al., 2016) and Yap Island (73%) (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on model estimates and supported by citations to other studies.

claim: The reported Zika outbreak in French Polynesia had an attack rate of 66%.
source: Based on this, around 65% of the local population were predicted to have been infected by ZIKV during the first wave in 2015, which is in the same range as the reported Zika outbreaks in French Polynesia (66%) (Cauchemez et al., 2016) and Yap Island (73%) (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cauchemez et al., 2016.

claim: The reported Zika outbreak in Yap Island had an attack rate of 73%.
source: Based on this, around 65% of the local population were predicted to have been infected by ZIKV during the first wave in 2015, which is in the same range as the reported Zika outbreaks in French Polynesia (66%) (Cauchemez et al., 2016) and Yap Island (73%) (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: It is possible that the high similarity of case definition to DENV, the concurrent CHIKV epidemic, and the low awareness of ZIKV at that time could have resulted in a significant number of ZIKV infections being classified as either dengue or chikungunya.
source: In the context of FSA, it is possible that the high similarity of case definition to DENV, the concurrent CHIKV epidemic, and the low awareness of ZIKV at that time could have resulted in a significant number of ZIKV infections being classified as either dengue or chikungunya.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The percentage of correctly diagnosed ZIKV infections and infected individuals seeking medical attention must have been exceptionally low (both lower than 20%).
source: Furthermore, based on our analysis, we would argue that the percentage of correctly diagnosed ZIKV infections and infected individuals seeking medical attention must have been exceptionally low (both lower than 20%).
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis of the observation rate.

claim: The age structure of notified cases showed a higher than expected incidence risk ratio (IRR) for individuals under the age of 4 years and a lower than expected risk for individuals aged + 50 years.
source: The age structure of notified cases showed a higher than expected incidence risk ratio (IRR) for individuals under the age of 4 years and a lower than expected risk for individuals aged + 50 years.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of age-stratified case data.

claim: During the Zika outbreak on Yap Island in 2007, all age classes, except the elderly, presented similar attack rates.
source: This contrasts the observation during the Zika outbreak on Yap Island in 2007, where all age classes, except the elderly, presented similar attack rates (Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Duffy et al., 2009.

claim: The signatures amongst the youngest and oldest individuals in FSA may reflect deficiencies and/or biases in local notified data.
source: It is therefore possible that the signatures amongst the youngest and oldest individuals in FSA may reflect deficiencies and/or biases in local notified data.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The increased risk in young children in 2016 may have been a result of increased awareness as well as the interventions by the WHO in the second year.
source: In fact, the increased risk in young children in 2016 may have been a result of increased awareness as well as the interventions by the WHO in the second year.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Temperature, with its direct influence on mosquito lifespan, aquatic development and extrinsic incubation period, was the key driver of seasonal oscillations in the transmission potential.
source: Similar to other studies in temperate and tropical settings, we found that temperature, with its direct influence on mosquito lifespan, aquatic development and extrinsic incubation period, was the key driver of seasonal oscillations in the transmission potential (Lourenço and Recker, 2014; Mordecai et al., 2016; Mourya et al., 2004; Feldstein et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is based on model results and supported by citations to other studies.

claim: Rainfall only seemed to play a marginal role in transmission potential.
source: Rainfall, on the other hand, only seemed to play a marginal role and we argue that it may be a relevant player for arboviral transmission mainly in tropical regions subject to intense rain seasons, such as areas in South East Asia (Cuong et al., 2011; Hii et al., 2012; Xuan et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is based on model results and supported by citations to studies in other regions.

claim: The correlations between climatic variables and case counts were inverted when addressed against the transmission potential.
source: We also noted that the correlations between climatic variables and case counts were inverted when addressed against the transmission potential.
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis.

claim: The 2015 epidemic peaked approximately 3 months after the estimated peak in the virus's transmission potential.
source: An interesting observation is that the 2015 epidemic peaked approximately 3 months after the estimated peak in the virus's transmission potential, whereas there was much higher synchrony during the second wave in 2016.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the relationship between R0 and case timing.

claim: There was much higher synchrony between transmission potential and epidemic peak during the second wave in 2016.
source: An interesting observation is that the 2015 epidemic peaked approximately 3 months after the estimated peak in the virus's transmission potential, whereas there was much higher synchrony during the second wave in 2016.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the relationship between R0 and case timing.

claim: The same behaviour has been described for the CHIKV outbreak in FSA in 2014–2015 and has been linked to highly discordant spatial distributions between the first two epidemics.
source: The same behaviour has been described for the CHIKV outbreak in FSA in 2014–2015 and which has been linked to highly discordant spatial distributions between the first two epidemics (Faria et al., 2016b).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Faria et al., 2016b.

claim: It is likely that similar spatial effects were present in FSA's ZIKV outbreaks.
source: It is likely that similar spatial effects (Kraemer et al., 2017) were present in FSA's ZIKV outbreaks.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation and supported by a citation.

claim: A phylogenetic analysis has proposed that the introduction of ZIKV into Bahia took place between March and September 2014.
source: A phylogenetic analysis has proposed that the introduction of ZIKV into Bahia took place between March and September 2014, although without direct evidence for its circulation in FSA at that time (Naccache et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Naccache et al., 2016.

claim: The estimated date of introduction in FSA was a few months after the proposed introduction into Bahia.
source: Our estimated date of introduction showed support for a date in early-mid December 2014, a few months after the proposed introduction into Bahia and just over 7 weeks before the first case of Zika was notified in FSA.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of model estimates with phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Similar periods between the first notification and estimated introduction often represent the time taken to complete one or more full transmission cycles before a cluster of cases is generated of sufficient size for detection by passive surveillance systems.
source: Similar periods between the first notification and estimated introduction often represent the time taken to complete one or more full transmission cycles (human-mosquito-human) before a cluster of cases is generated of sufficient size for detection by passive surveillance systems (Lourenço and Recker, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lourenço and Recker, 2014.

claim: The number of ZIKV infections during the first 2 months after notification could have amounted to over 2700 actual cases.
source: Given our estimated observation rate, however, the number of ZIKV infections during this time could have amounted to over 2700 actual cases.
evidence: The claim is based on applying the estimated observation rate to notified cases.

claim: The Micareta festival may have played a role in igniting the exponential phase of the epidemic by facilitating human-vector mixing as well as a more rapid geographical expansion.
source: In April, the number of cases increased rapidly, coinciding with the Micareta festival, which we argue may have played a role in igniting the exponential phase of the epidemic by facilitating human-vector mixing as well as a more rapid geographical expansion.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: Without the possibility of externally acquired infections, local extinction was very likely by 2017 due to the high levels of herd-immunity.
source: Without the possibility of externally acquired infections, local extinction was very likely by 2017 due to the high levels of herd-immunity.
evidence: The claim is based on model projections.

claim: The projections corroborated the conclusions of previous modelling studies that suggest a weak endemic potential for ZIKV after the initial exhaustion of the susceptible pool.
source: When explicitly modelling the importation of infectious cases our projections for the next two decades corroborated the conclusions of previous modelling studies that suggest a weak endemic potential for ZIKV after the initial exhaustion of the susceptible pool (Ferguson et al., 2016; Kucharski et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on model projections and supported by citations to other studies.

claim: The future epidemic behaviour is strongly dependent on the frequency of re-introductions, where sporadic and unpredictable epidemics could still be in the order of hundreds of cases.
source: However, our simulations also showed that the future epidemic behaviour is strongly dependent on the frequency of re-introductions, where sporadic and unpredictable epidemics could still be in the order of hundreds of cases.
evidence: The claim is based on stochastic model projections.

claim: Given the estimated observation rate for the 2015–2017 epidemic, passive surveillance systems are unlikely to fully detect the scale and occurrence of small epidemics.
source: Furthermore, given our estimated observation rate for the 2015–2017 epidemic, passive surveillance systems are unlikely to fully detect the scale and occurrence of such small epidemics, missing their actual public health impact, and as such efforts should thus be placed to improve ZIKV detection and diagnosis in order to optimize the local reporting rates and potential for control.
evidence: The claim is based on the estimated observation rate and its implications.

claim: With a total of over 10,000 live births in 2015 in FSA, the crude estimate for the risk of Zika-associated MC per pregnancy was below 4 cases per 100,000 individuals in a generalized population under an attack rate of 65%.
source: With a total of over 10,000 live births in 2015 in FSA, our crude estimate for the risk of Zika-associated MC per pregnancy was below 4 cases per 100,000 individuals in a generalized population under an attack rate of 65%.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of MC cases and estimated attack rate.

claim: The risk of Zika-associated MC is extremely low when compared to other known viral-associated complications, such as those caused by infections by cytomegalovirus (CMV) and the rubella virus (RV).
source: As discussed elsewhere (Cauchemez et al., 2016), this risk is extremely low when compared to other known viral-associated complications, such as those caused by infections by cytomegalovirus (CMV) and the rubella virus (RV) (De Santis et al., 2006; Naing et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to other studies.

claim: What makes the ZIKV a public health concern is not necessarily the per pregnancy risk of neurological complications, but rather the combination of low risk with very high attack rates.
source: It is therefore crucial to reiterate that what makes the ZIKV a public health concern is not necessarily the per pregnancy risk of neurological complications, but rather the combination of low risk with very high attack rates.
evidence: The claim is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: For the Yap Island epidemic, no microcephaly cases have been reported.
source: For the Yap Island epidemic, no microcephaly cases have been reported.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the manuscript text.

claim: With an estimated 24 births per 1000 females and using an overall risk of approximately 0.4% per pregnancy, only 0–3 cases per 100,000 individuals would have been expected in Yap Island.
source: With an estimated 24 births per 1000 females (census 2000 as in (Duffy et al., 2009)) and using an overall risk of approximately 0.4% per pregnancy, only 0–3 cases per 100,000 individuals would have been expected.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using cited birth rate data and estimated risk.

claim: The island's small population size (7391 individuals) together with a general baseline of 0–2 microcephaly cases per 100,000 in many areas of the world would explain the absence of reported cases in Yap Island.
source: However, the island's small population size (7391 individuals (Duffy et al., 2009)) together with a general baseline of 0–2 microcephaly cases per 100,000 in many areas of the world (Johansson et al., 2016; Butler, 2016; EUROCAT, 2003) would explain the absence of reported cases.
evidence: The claim is based on cited population data and baseline MC rates.

claim: A variety of birth defects have been found to be statistically associated with Zika virus infection during pregnancy, of which MC is one possible outcome.
source: It is also important to consider that a variety of birth defects have been found to be statistically associated with Zika virus infection during pregnancy, of which MC is one possible outcome.
evidence: The claim is stated as general knowledge.

claim: While the risk for birth defects per pregnancy is consistently reported to be high, estimations for the risk of MC vary considerably.
source: While the risk for birth defects per pregnancy is consistently reported to be high, estimations for the risk of MC vary considerably.
evidence: The claim is stated as general knowledge.

claim: Recent clinical trials suggested that the risk of Zika-associated MC could be an order of magnitude higher than the estimate reported in this or other previous studies.
source: For example, recent clinical trials (Honein et al., 2017; Brasil et al., 2016) suggested that the risk of Zika-associated MC could be an order of magnitude higher than the estimate reported in this or other previous studies (Cauchemez et al., 2016; Duffy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical trials.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that viral or host genetic background, as well as the pre-exposition to other arboviruses may influence the absolute risk experienced by local populations or cohorts.
source: Alternatively, viral or host genetic background, as well as the pre-exposition to other arboviruses may influence the absolute risk experienced by local populations or cohorts.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: It is plausible that the observation rate changed upon official guidelines and that the capacity to accurately diagnose and report Zika infections could have been lower in 2015 compared subsequent years.
source: It is therefore plausible that the observation rate changed upon official guidelines and that the capacity to accurately diagnose and report Zika infections could have been lower in 2015 compared subsequent years.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: When allowing for a possible change in the observation rate for 2016 and onwards, a similar observation rate for 2015 (0.0039 versus 0.0034) was found as well as a similar attack rate between the two model variants.
source: To explore this, we reran our fitting approach allowing for a possible change in the observation rate for 2016 and onwards (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and found a similar observation rate for 2015 (0.0039 versus 0.0034) as well as a similar attack rate between the two model variants.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The revised diagnosis guidelines may have increased the proportion correctly diagnosed while the proportion of symptomatic individuals visiting medical facilities did not change.
source: It is hard to discern where the positive changes took place, but we suggest the revised diagnosis guidelines may have increased the proportion correctly diagnosed while the proportion of symptomatic individuals visiting medical facilities did not change.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: It is tempting to speculate that the 2015/2016 imbalance in reporting may have been a general phenomenon across Brazil.
source: It is also tempting to speculate that the 2015/2016 imbalance in reporting may have been a general phenomenon across Brazil.
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: It is possible that FSA is a good example of states and urban centres that may have witnessed larger epidemics than reported in 2015.
source: As described elsewhere, it is thus possible that FSA is a good example of states and urban centres that may have witnessed larger epidemics than reported in 2015 (de Oliveira et al., 2017).

claim: Low MC risk with very high attack rates makes ZIKV a public health concern, which could explain why most MC reports at the level of the country were in 2015.
source: This, together with our conclusion that low MC risk with very high attack rates makes ZIKV a public health concern, could explain why most MC reports at the level of the country were in 2015 (de Oliveira et al., 2017), although for many regions the total reported number of ZIKV cases may have been surprisingly small that year.

claim: Control and surveillance of ZIKV should be boosted and focused in periods of high temperature and during major social events.
source: Our results imply that control and surveillance of ZIKV should be boosted and focused in periods of high temperature and during major social events.

claim: These factors could identify windows of opportunity for local interventions to mitigate ZIKV introduction and transmission and should be transferable to other areas for which both temperature data and community event schedules are available.

source: We further confirm that the high transmission potential of ZIKV in urban centres can lead to the exhaustion of the local susceptible pool, which will in turn dictate the long-term epidemic and endemic behaviour of the virus.
evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the study results.

claim: Local sporadic occurrences could still have important public health consequences, and much better diagnostics and reporting rates are required for local authorities to detect and respond to such events in the near future.
